title: QR code menu restaurant vs calling in: what works better
seoTitle: QR code menu restaurant vs calling in | ROAL
description: Compare a QR code menu with calling in by cost, order accuracy, upsells, and setup so you can pick the better fit for your restaurant.
question: Should I use a QR code menu restaurant setup or keep taking orders by phone?
answer: A QR code menu restaurant setup is good for guests sitting in the dining room, but it does not replace phone orders, menu questions, reservations, or callers who prefer to talk. Most independent restaurants do best with both: QR menus for table browsing and a phone host for pickup, delivery, and questions.
summary: You’ll be able to choose a QR menu, phone orders, or both based on how your restaurant actually gets business.
intro:
A QR code menu restaurant setup helps guests browse without waiting for a server to bring a menu. Calling in is better when the customer wants to place a pickup or delivery order, ask about hours, or make sure the kitchen got the notes right.

For most independent restaurants, the real question is not QR code menu or phone. It is which jobs should happen on the table and which should happen on the phone. If you want the phone side handled for you, ROAL can answer the restaurant’s calls, take orders from the live menu, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

sections.h2: When does a QR code menu restaurant setup make sense?
sections.body:
A QR code menu restaurant setup is useful when customers are already inside and mainly need to read the menu. It works well for dine-in places where people want to browse items, check prices, and place their own order with a server nearby.

It also helps if your menu changes often. A QR code can point to a page you update once, instead of printing new menus every time you change a special. That said, QR menus do not solve phone calls. Someone still has to answer, explain the menu, and take orders from people driving, working, or calling ahead.

A simple owner checklist:
- Keep the QR menu current with prices and sold-out items.
- Make the font easy to read on a small phone screen.
- Include allergy notes and house specials.
- Add a clear phone number for pickup or questions.
- Test it on an older phone before you print a stack of table tents.

If your guests often call to order, a QR menu should be one tool, not the only one.

sections.h2: What do phone orders do better than QR menus?
sections.body:
Phone orders still win when speed, clarity, and human help matter. A caller can say, "I want two chicken parm dinners, one with no cheese, and add a small salad," and the host can repeat it back, confirm the ready time, and collect the caller’s name and phone.

That matters for pickup and delivery. It also matters for families, older customers, and anyone who is not standing in the restaurant looking at a menu on a screen. On the phone, your team can answer questions like parking, hours, address, and what comes on a dish.

Here is a simple comparison:

| Job | QR menu | Phone order |
|---|---|---|
| Browse a menu at the table | Good | Possible, but not ideal |
| Take a detailed pickup order | Weak | Strong |
| Ask about sold-out items | Weak | Strong |
| Handle allergies or manager requests | Weak | Strong |
| Quote a ready time | No | Yes |

ROAL is built for those phone jobs. It takes items, sizes, modifiers, and notes from the live menu and sends the order to the kitchen screen.

sections.h2: How do the costs compare for a small restaurant?
sections.body:
Costs are where many owners get stuck. A QR code menu can be cheap to start, but it does not automatically lower the cost of taking phone orders. If you still answer calls yourself, that time is still there.

Use a simple example and plug in your own numbers:
- Say you get 40 phone orders a month.
- Say your average order is $28.
- If an outside service charges a fixed monthly fee, you pay that whether the phone rings or not.
- If delivery apps take roughly 15-30% commission, a $28 order can lose about $4.20 to $8.40 before food and labor. That is just an example; use your own order size.

ROAL uses pay-per-completed-order pricing: $0.90 for a confirmed order that reaches the kitchen screen. There is no monthly fee, no setup fee, no per-minute fee, and no contract. Calls, questions, and test calls are free.

That makes the math easy. If you want to compare your current setup, use [the AI phone host cost calculator](/tools/phone-host-cost-calculator) and swap in your own order count.

sections.h2: How should you split QR menus and phone orders?
sections.body:
The cleanest setup is usually this: let the QR menu handle dine-in browsing, and let the phone handle pickup, delivery, questions, and reservation requests. That way each channel does the job it is best at.

A practical setup for a pizza shop, deli, or family restaurant:
1. Put the QR code on tables, counters, and takeout flyers.
2. Keep the menu readable and current.
3. Keep the phone number large on the homepage and Google profile.
4. Use the phone for people who want to order while driving or leaving work.
5. Make sure the phone path and the QR path show the same prices and items.

If your team is short-staffed, this split matters even more. A QR menu can reduce the need to explain every item at the table, while an AI phone host can catch the callers who would otherwise ring and ring.

If you want the basics of a good restaurant phone setup, [the phone number should appear in a few key places](/blog/restaurant-phone-number-everywhere).

sections.h2: What should you tell customers on the phone and on the menu?
sections.body:
The wording should be simple and direct. On the QR menu, tell guests what it is for: "Scan to browse the menu and order at the table." On the phone side, say what happens next: "We take pickup and delivery orders by phone during business hours."

Use short script lines your staff or phone host can repeat:
- "I can take that order now and give you the ready time."
- "We are out of that item right now, but I can offer the closest option."
- "For allergy-sensitive questions, I’m sending this to the kitchen team."
- "If you’d like to place a pickup order, I can do that here."

For a plain-English menu note, try this: "Prices and availability can change. Please call for pickup or delivery orders." That tells guests where to go without sounding stiff.

ROAL can also answer common questions about hours, address, parking, and the menu. If a question is too tricky, it goes to staff with a summary, so you do not have to repeat the same answer over and over.

sections.h2: How do you keep QR menus and phone info from conflicting?
sections.body:
The biggest problem is not choosing QR menus or calling in. It is having different prices, different specials, or different hours in different places. That creates confusion fast.

Use this check before you print QR stickers or go live with a phone setup:
- Same hours on the menu, website, and Google listing.
- Same address and parking note everywhere.
- Same sold-out items across the menu and phone line.
- Same pickup name and phone number format.
- One person owns updates when prices change.

If you use ROAL, the owner pastes the restaurant website, Google Maps link, or "Name, City" at /try, and it reads public pages to build a phone host in about a minute. You can test-call it in the browser, then claim the host and forward the restaurant’s existing number to it. The restaurant keeps its own number, and forwarding can be turned off any time.

For the forwarding part, always confirm the exact code with your carrier or phone system and test it with a call. Codes vary, so do not assume one setup works everywhere.

sections.h2: What should you do this week if you want both options to work?
sections.body:
Start small. Do not rebuild your whole ordering process at once. Use QR menus where guests are already seated, and improve the phone path where missed calls or long hold times are costing you orders.

A simple one-week plan:
1. Check every place your phone number appears.
2. Update your QR menu with current prices and sold-out items.
3. Write one short phone greeting for pickup and delivery.
4. Decide who handles allergy questions and manager requests.
5. Test your call forwarding with a real call from a cell phone.

If you want the phone side handled without hiring more staff, [build a free test host from your website](/try). You can hear how it answers, see the live ticket flow, and decide whether it fits your shop before you forward anything.

The goal is not to replace every guest interaction. It is to make sure dine-in customers can self-serve with the QR menu, while phone customers still get a clear path to order.

takeaways: QR menus are best for dine-in browsing; phone orders are better for pickup, delivery, and questions.
A QR code menu restaurant setup should not replace your phone number or your staff’s call process.
Use the same hours, prices, and sold-out items everywhere to avoid confusion.
ROAL can answer calls, take orders, and send clean tickets to the kitchen screen.

faq.q: Is a QR code menu better than taking orders by phone?
faq.a: Not for every job. QR menus are useful for table browsing, but phone orders are better for detailed pickup orders, questions, and reservations. Most restaurants do best with both: QR for dine-in and phone for callers who want help.

faq.q: Do QR menus reduce phone calls?
faq.a: Sometimes, but they do not replace them. Guests still call about hours, parking, sold-out items, and pickup orders. If you want those calls handled well, a phone host can cover that side while the QR menu handles the table.

faq.q: How do I set up call forwarding for my restaurant phone?
faq.a: It depends on your carrier or phone system. Many landlines use *72 to forward all calls and *73 to turn it off, while some mobile carriers use codes like **21*number# or **61*number#; always confirm with your carrier and test the call. Business VoIP systems usually let you set this in the web portal.

faq.q: Can ROAL take card payments over the phone?
faq.a: No. ROAL does not take card numbers over the phone. Payment happens at pickup or however the restaurant already takes it, and the host focuses on getting the order right and sending a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.
